title: COP31 ends in failure
transcript:
Speaker 1: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music, and more.
Isabella Higgins: Good morning. Welcome to AM. It's Monday, the 23rd of November. I'm Isabella Higgins, coming to you from Nanal Country in Canberra. Major global climate talks have collapsed without a deal after a fierce debate about the future of fossil fuels. COP31 in Tokyo ran into overtime after nations failed to reach consensus in the longest deliberation in the UN Summit's 30-year history. The deadlock came as the Saudi-led oil-producing nations fought against the mention of fossil fuels in the draft agreement, while the European Union insisted it was too weak. The Irish Minister for Climate, Dara O'Brien, was representing the EU.
Dara O'Brien: We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that is not even mentioning fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time, and we will not accept a cop that greenwashes fossil fuel.
Isabella Higgins: Australia's Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen was in charge of negotiations and has described the outcome as very disappointing. Environment reporter Romy Stevens joined me for more in the studio. Romy, why did these talks not achieve an outcome?
Romy Stevens: These negotiations really started to gather pace last Monday. That was when we saw the first draft of a text released, and within that, it explicitly called for the immediate transition away from fossil fuels. Now, whilst there were disagreements over that initial text, it was quite lengthy. It pretty much had everything that every nation wanted. So, there was no doubt it was going to be 
refined. A lot of people welcomed the stronger language that was used within that text. Then we got to Thursday a few days later, and the second draft text came out and it had removed any reference whatsoever to the use or the transition away from fossil fuels. And this is where things really started to unravel. It's it was widely reported that Saudi Arabia was leading the push on behalf of fossil fuel producing nations to remove reference to the burning of coal, oil and gas. And then, on the other hand, the likes of Panama and the European Union were pushing for that to be included. So, we then got to the weekend and that's where the talks really started to grind to a halt and it started to blow out into overtime. Uh and it wasn't until yesterday afternoon, Sunday afternoon, Australian time, where the final draft was released. Now, the leadership in Turkey and Australia tried to appease nations by including reference 
to commitments that had been made in previous years at previous cops where countries had agreed to move away from fossil fuels. But ultimately, that wasn't enough, and there were a large number of nations that just said they couldn't agree to a deal that didn't include fossil fuels, which scientists say is driving climate change. And ultimately, we didn't see a deal go through at all.
Isabella Higgins: And Australia has a a real stake in the game here. Australia was the head of negotiations at COP31. Where does this leave, Chris Bowen?
Romy Stevens: Yeah, I think it's important to first acknowledge that these talks are extraordinarily difficult. You have to reach a consensus from almost 200 nations that attend. That includes developing countries and small island nations on the front line of climate change, as well as fossil fuel producing nations who depend on coal, oil and gas to strengthen their economies. And so these talks often go down to the wire, they often blow out over time, but 
really having not reached an agreement is just extraordinarily consequential. And I think what's more is that countries couldn't even agree to things that they agreed on in years gone by. Um, and so there are real questions around where the world is at and what role these conferences play going forward. And I think there's also questions over why the leadership in both Turkey and Australia didn't prioritize building consensus on fossil fuels 
earlier. Perhaps they knew it would be a sticking point and so they decided to really focus uh and hone in on pushing for electrification. Um and Chris Bowen himself welcomed that more than 90 countries signed their their electrification pledge, but he's expressed his deep disappointment that they were unable to reach a main agreement.
Chris Bowen: take my share of responsibility ultimately, um you know, people can judge uh what could have been done or couldn't have been done. Ultimately, it's a party-driven process and ultimately, parties chose not to seek and agree.
Isabella Higgins: Climate change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen, and before him, our reporter Romy Stevens. Alison Reeve is the energy and Climate Change program director at the Graton Institute. She joined me a short time ago for more on this. Alison, thanks for your time this morning on AM. First, can I get your reaction to these failed talks at COP 31?
Alison Reeve: Thanks, Isabella. I mean, this this cop was always going to have, I think, some fairly unbridgeable questions. Like one thing that has plagued cops in the past, I think is that there's been a lot of papering over of cracks, particularly around things like finance for developing countries, but also around what to say about fossil fuels. It's becoming increasingly difficult to have a decision that pleases both the Petro states and also the states who want to see more action to phrase out fossil fuels. And I think that is really what has come to ahead at this particular cop.
Isabella Higgins: And what does this tell you about broadly about the direction of global energy, climate policy?
Alison Reeve: Yeah, I think it sort of we are we are dealing with those issues in the midst of quite a difficult time. There's a lot of other things going on at the same time, whether that's, you know, fuel crisis, other geopolitical issues and so on. And I think what it really shows is that governments don't really have the luxury anymore of just dealing with one crisis at the time at a time. They are just going to have to get good at 
keeping their climate agendas going at the same time that other stuff is unfolding. What that means is, you know, when we talk about action between countries and also within particular countries, we should be looking for things like electrification, for example, that allow us to solve both problems at the same time, allow us to deal with a fuel crisis and deal with climate. 
Allow us to insulate ourselves from geopolitics and deal with climate at the same time.
Isabella Higgins: COP was always about bringing small nations together with bigger nations and trying to create a global agenda for climate. But these failed talks, what do you think that means for the future of the UN summit? Do you think less nations are going to want to participate? Where does it leave us?
Alison Reeve: Look, COP COP is a really cumbersome and slow process, but it's the only one that we've got to try and get every country to take it action to address climate change. I think one thing that we've been starting to see emerging over the past couple of years are things like climate clubs where groups of like-minded countries get together and agree to cooperation between themselves. We've seen country-to-country deals like the one that Australia signed with Korea last week. I think increasingly those are going to be the things where we actually get the momentum to be able to um 
show that action is taking place. But the thing is that we're, I think, really going to have to solve with this is I think particularly if we are seeing this as a forum for large countries and for small countries, we need to grapple with the fact that small countries do not have the same capacity to do the level of implementation that large countries are doing because they don't have the money. 
And large countries have consistently failed to to bridge that for them.
Isabella Higgins: And where does this leave Australia who fought to be really involved in this COP 31, ultimately it it did happen in Turkey, yeah, but Australia was head of negotiations here.
Alison Reeve: They were. I mean, look, I I think it was it was probably a pretty a pretty tough job. It was always going to be a very difficult cop. You know, I I think the best we can say is that we gave it the very best go that we could. We didn't get all the way to the presidency outcome that perhaps Australia and Turkey would have liked. 
But the process will keep going. I think the thing that we've demonstrated is that Australia can be a player internationally. It was certainly not us that wrecked the decision. So, you know, I I think from Australia's perspective, it's really back home, back to work to, you know, start to reduce our own emissions and roll on to to Ethiopia next year and hope that we can make a positive contribution there.
Isabella Higgins: Alison Reeve, the energy and climate change program director at the Graton Institute. Thanks for your time this morning.
Alison Reeve: Thanks, Isabella.
Isabella Higgins: Well, pressure is on the government as it races to get key legislation passed before Parliament's summer break. The digital duty of care bill will be front and center with the last sitting week of the year set to be dominated by talks of AI and its possible harms. For more, here's political reporter Isabella Tolhurst.
Isabella Tolhurst: Big tech under scrutiny. Australia's politicians from across the political divide are cracking down on what they say is the free reign tech companies have enjoyed for years. Green Senator Sarah Hansen Young says it's time Australians take back control.
Sarah Hansen Young: For too long, big tech has carried on as if there are a special category. Australian businesses don't have the same type of Laze faire attitudes to laws and regulations the way big tech does.
Isabella Tolhurst: The government's digital duty of care laws, which will put an onus on platforms to foreseeable harm online, is looking set to be strengthened through the Greens amendments that enable Australians to sue tech companies if they are harmed.
Sarah Hansen Young: I'm hopeful that we are getting somewhere with the government. We've seen them open the door to allowing for individuals and organizations to be able to take big tech to court.
Isabella Tolhurst: The government also appears to be taking feedback on board. Communications Minister Anika Wells confirming small businesses will be exempt from the duty of care after the Chamber of Commerce and Industry voiced concerns that local businesses would be caught up in the laws and required to prevent harm on their websites. But Senator Hansen Young says that was never the intention of the bill.
Sarah Hansen Young: This is about the big tech giants. This is about the social media giants who have made billions of dollars of profit off a system that they know is addictive.
Isabella Tolhurst: AI is a major issue on the global political agenda. Tech companies are being put on notice for a range of reasons. Donald Trump even demanding that AI companies do not build data centers overseas. Something Deputy Prime Minister Richard Miles said would be bad news back home.
Richard Miles: We would like to see that investment in Australia, of course, you know, it's it's not at any cost. We we need to be doing it on our terms.
Isabella Tolhurst: Those terms are being made clearer by the Australian government, who is promising to legislate national AI standards early next year. And a major speech in Parliament by foreign Minister Penny Wong will this week elevate AI as a national security challenge, concerns about foreign interference shared by O CEO Mike Burgess on 960 minutes last night.
Mike Burgess: If we don't understand who the owner is or there's foreign money and actually it's not declared where that money is coming from, then yes, we might have a problem because that is potentially acts of foreign interference.
Isabella Tolhurst: While the door has largely been thrown open to investment, he warns malicious foreign actors could seek influence over Australian data centers.
Mike Burgess: It could actually be they're looking to have some form of ownership control over that infrastructure, which they could then use for nefarious reasons, which gives them access to the technology or the information inside that data center.
Isabella Tolhurst: In her speech on Tuesday, Senator Wong is also set to lay out plans for Australia to become a world leader in shaping the international order on AI safety. But in a fast moving space, Australia may already be on the back foot.
Isabella Tolhurst: Isabella Tolhurst reporting. Well, amid a cost of living crisis, working Australians pushed to the brink and now skipping essential medicines and healthcare just to make ends meet. These are the findings of consumer health forums, major new survey where almost half of all respondents said they had gone without something they needed this year.
Any guest has more.
Isabella Higgins: To hear about how it's health policies are working, the federal government funds the Consumer Health Forum to commission surveys across the country. Its CEO, Elizabeth Devaney, is today releasing the latest results.
Elizabeth Devaney: Nearly six in 10 Australians say they put off or avoided dental care at some point, and the most common reason is the cost. And that's particularly those people experiencing financial stress. So about 77% of people who are experiencing some financial stress are saying that they miss or delay care because they can't afford the doctors or the script, because instead they've got to pay for petrol or perhaps their mortgage.
Isabella Higgins: And Dr. Devaney adds that affordability isn't the only barrier.
Elizabeth Devaney: When we see young people reporting higher unmet needs and also saying that they don't feel that they were listen to respected as well perhaps as older people have been, we see women reporting poor mental health, delaying care more often, and experiencing more discrimination. Um, there are many groups we can see in our surveys who aren't getting the same benefits from these reforms as others.
Isabella Higgins: Health economist Professor Dennis Petri is from Monash University.
Dennis Petri: It didn't come too much of a surprise, you know, it's always been an issue there, but I suppose it's become more acute definitely, uh, in the last year with interest rates rising and cost of living pressures, um, you know, putting households under stress. And so, you know, when that happens, you know, they often have to make hard choices.
Isabella Higgins: Professor Petri believes making wealthier people pay more would free up access including in urgent care and bulk billing clinics.
Dennis Petri: Having a look at, you know, the extent to which, you know, which we means test things and try and provide better access for people who, you know, are more under financial strain.
Isabella Higgins: Professor Petri specializes in health workforce modeling, and he says GP clinics opening hours and roles of workers are restrictive.
Dennis Petri: Think about how we have a flexible healthcare system and not only rely on GPs, um, but also, you know, make the most of our other healthcare professionals who bring, you know, skills, um, that can improve people's health.
Isabella Higgins: And that is the direction the government has been trying to head in, isn't it? Under the the policy called um My Medicare? Is it working?
Dennis Petri: Yeah, I wouldn't say that it's, you know, all guns blazing, but I'd say that, you know, there's slow progress there.
Isabella Higgins: In a statement, the health Minister Mark Butler told AM the government has reduced PBS medicine costs, provided free tele health, 137 urgent care clinics, and fully bulk billing GP practices have almost doubled in a year. Mr. Butler says 97% of Australians live within 20 minutes of those practices, with the biggest jump in rural areas. And the national oral health plan is being progressed with states and territories, the dental sector and other key stakeholders, to support a coordinated national approach to improving oral health outcomes.
Isabella Higgins: A guest reporting.
Isabella Higgins: As the theater industry grapples with new ways to sell tickets in the cost of living crisis, the country's second largest ballet company is trying a fresh take on an old favorite. Queensland Ballet is importing world first costume design and choreography to reimagine the well-known classic, The Nutcracker. Stephanie Smale has more.
Stephanie Smale: For British choreographer Derek Dean, the opportunity to tweak a Christmas classic in Queensland took some thought.
Derek Dean: My first impression was what what can I do with it? What how can I change it? How can I make it different? If I'm going to do it, um, we have to find a different way of doing it.
Derek Dean: One, stay, one.
Stephanie Smale: But working up ideas with the world renowned set and costume designer Lez Brotherston, who's also UK based, excited him.
Derek Dean: I have pirates, I have ice walls, I have ice creatures, uh, icicles, all sorts of different, uh, characters within the ballet, uh, to make it unique for this production.
Isabella Higgins: Audiences will still hear the famous Tchaikovsky score and recognize the story of Clara and her Christmas Eve dream. But Derek Dean says this version has some darker beats.
Derek Dean: You know, dreams go up and down. Dreams go in and out. Sometimes there's slight nightmares, sometimes there's sweet. So I'd also try to put that into the production as well.
Isabella Higgins: Queensland Ballet has juggled a string of changes since Li Chun-In's departure, the resignation of long-serving executive director Dilshani Weerasinghe, the latest shift. It's been tough financially, too, with budget cuts and job losses.
Derek Dean: You know, financials will always be a thing, but it's just how you overcome that. And I think that's with the magic of being on stage. You know, that's where you go. This is what this was really worth it.
Isabella Higgins: That's Queensland Ballet's artistic director, Ivan Hillo Teega. He says the new look nutcracker is about business as well as beauty.
Derek Dean: This is a world premiere. We are the only company doing this version. And, you know, hopefully people will realize and will travel the world.
Isabella Higgins: It is a big budget production. Is it the case of you need to spend big to earn big?
Derek Dean: Completely, completely. This is the long run. This is something that I think also identifies that where Queensland Ballet is and where it's going.
Isabella Higgins: It's been a global effort to pull the new take on the nutcracker together with Lez Brotherston's designs delivered by a team across Australia and overseas. Lauren Jackson is Queensland Ballet's head of costume.
Derek Dean: Obviously, Lez, who's overseas in the UK, we've also got Robert who's making our masks in the UK. We've got another lady down in South Australia who's been building the soldiers and the rats. And then I've got a lady on the Sunshine Coast, a couple of people in Brisbane as freelancers and obviously my team in here, nearly 30 people.
Isabella Higgins: Lauren Jackson says it's taken a year to pull it all together.
Derek Dean: I mean, you can't go past the tutu really, can you? But there are so many beautiful pieces in here.
Isabella Higgins: The Nutcracker opens in Brisbane in December.
Stephanie Smale: Steph Smale with that report and that's AM for today. Thanks for your company. I'm Isabella Higgins.
Sam Hawley: Hi, it's Sam Hawley here, host of the ABC News daily podcast. Measles is officially back in the United States. With America losing the elimination status, it gained more than a quarter of a century ago. So is Donald Trump's handpicked health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., to blame? Today, Dr. Peter Hotez, professor at the Baylor College of Medicine, on the anti-vaccination movement that's led to the measles resurgence. Look for the ABC News daily podcast on ABC Listen.
